title: Experimental Physics and Measurement
subject: Physics

cards.prompt: What is Measurand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measurand is the physical quantity intended to be measured, defined with the relevant object, conditions, and time or averaging convention. Ambiguous definitions can make measurements disagree even when instruments operate correctly.
required_concepts: Precisely defined target quantity with conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating an unspecified instrument number as a complete definition of the physical target.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measurement model relates recorded inputs and correction quantities to the intended measurand. It makes calibration, environmental dependence, and assumptions explicit rather than assuming every raw sensor value equals the target directly.
required_concepts: Map observations and corrections to the measurand.
major_error_concepts: Equating a sensor output with the physical target without its conversion model.

cards.prompt: What is Operational Definition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An operational definition specifies how a quantity is realized or measured in a procedure. It should connect to the physical concept while making choices such as thresholds, averaging windows, and reference points explicit.
required_concepts: Procedure defines the realized measurement meaning.
major_error_concepts: Changing a threshold while claiming the measured quantity's definition stayed exactly the same.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A unit supplies the reference scale for a numerical physical quantity. A numerical value without its unit can be ambiguous, and unit conversion changes numbers while preserving the underlying quantity.
required_concepts: Reference scale paired with numerical value.
major_error_concepts: Changing a unit label without changing the corresponding number where conversion requires it.

cards.prompt: What is Dimensional Consistency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dimensional consistency requires quantities added or equated in a physical model to have matching dimensions. It can expose errors but does not prove the model's coefficients, assumptions, or physical interpretation are correct.
required_concepts: Compatible dimensions constrain physical equations.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an equation is physically established solely because its units match.

cards.prompt: What is Calibration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Calibration establishes a relation between an instrument indication and reference values under specified conditions, including uncertainty. Applying a calibration can correct readings, but does not guarantee validity outside the calibrated range or conditions.
required_concepts: Reference-based indication-to-quantity relation.
Range and conditions matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one calibration makes an instrument accurate forever at every input and environment.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Reference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measurement reference is a value, object, or procedure used to compare or establish an instrument response. It carries its own uncertainty and conditions rather than functioning as an automatically exact truth.
required_concepts: Comparison reference with stated uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Assigning zero uncertainty to every reference merely because it is called a standard.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Traceability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement traceability links a result to a stated reference through a documented chain of calibrations with uncertainty contributions. Naming a reference without the linking evidence does not by itself establish that chain.
required_concepts: Documented calibration chain to a stated reference.
major_error_concepts: Claiming traceability solely from a manufacturer's name without the relevant calibration linkage.

cards.prompt: What is Accuracy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Accuracy describes closeness of a measured result to the intended reference or true quantity under the chosen interpretation. It differs from precision: tightly clustered measurements can all share a substantial offset.
required_concepts: Closeness to the target distinct from clustering.
major_error_concepts: Concluding repeated identical readings prove closeness to the true measurand.

cards.prompt: What is Precision? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Precision describes the closeness of repeated measurement results under stated conditions. It concerns spread, not the absence of systematic effects or agreement with a reference value.
required_concepts: Repeat-result dispersion under specified conditions.
major_error_concepts: Calling low scatter proof that calibration bias is negligible.

cards.prompt: What is Repeatability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Repeatability concerns measurement variation when the procedure, instrument, operator, and conditions are kept as similar as specified over a short interval. It is narrower than variation across independently changed laboratories or setups.
required_concepts: Variation under closely held measurement conditions.
major_error_concepts: Calling same-setup repeatability a demonstration of agreement across every other laboratory.

cards.prompt: What is Reproducibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reproducibility concerns agreement or variation under declared changed conditions, such as instruments, operators, or laboratories. The changed conditions must be named because the word alone does not define one universal test.
required_concepts: Agreement across specified changed conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming broad reproducibility from repeated calculations on the same unchanged data alone.

cards.prompt: What is Random Measurement Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A random measurement effect produces unpredictable variation described statistically across repetitions under stated conditions. Averaging can reduce some random contributions, but only according to their dependence and distribution, not automatically as one over the square root of every record count.
required_concepts: Statistical variation with assumptions about repetition.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all repeated records are independent simply because the numbers differ.

cards.prompt: What is Systematic Measurement Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A systematic effect shifts or distorts measurements in a structured way, such as a persistent offset or environmental dependence. Repetition alone need not reduce it; correction and residual uncertainty require information about the mechanism.
required_concepts: Structured persistent measurement influence.
major_error_concepts: Assuming collecting more identical-condition measurements removes a fixed calibration offset.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement uncertainty characterizes the dispersion of values reasonably associated with the reported measurand under the model and available information. It is not a guarantee that every value in a printed interval is equally likely or that the exact error is known.
required_concepts: Quantified uncertainty about the measurand.
Distinct from known error or uniform probability.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting every uncertainty interval as an equal-probability set without a distribution model.

cards.prompt: What is Error and Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement error is the difference between a measured value and a specified reference or true value, while uncertainty describes what is known about the measurand or error contributions. A result can have quantified uncertainty even when its actual error is unknown.
required_concepts: Actual discrepancy differs from uncertainty about the result.
major_error_concepts: Equating an uncertainty estimate with the exact signed error of the measurement.

cards.prompt: What is Estimator Bias? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Estimator bias is the repeated-sampling expectation of an estimator minus its target quantity. It is not the realized error of one estimate, though a known systematic measurement effect can contribute to bias under an appropriate model.
required_concepts: Expectation minus estimand, not one-sample discrepancy.
major_error_concepts: Calling any single off-target estimate proof that its estimator has nonzero repeated-sampling bias.

cards.prompt: What is Instrument Resolution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Instrument resolution is the smallest indication change that can be distinguished under specified conditions. It differs from accuracy and may be much finer than the uncertainty from calibration, noise, or environmental effects.
required_concepts: Distinguishable indication increment.
Not the same as total accuracy.
major_error_concepts: Taking the number of displayed digits as proof of equally many accurate digits.

cards.prompt: What is Sensitivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sensitivity is the change in instrument output per change in the input quantity near a specified operating point. High sensitivity does not by itself guarantee low uncertainty if noise or instability also increases.
required_concepts: Local output-to-input response slope.
major_error_concepts: Equating a large output gain automatically with a more accurate measurement.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Range? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement range is the input span over which an instrument or model has specified behavior. Dynamic range compares large and small usable signals under stated limits; neither is established by extrapolating beyond documented response.
required_concepts: Usable input span and signal-scale limits.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a calibration at midrange certifies untested extreme inputs automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Instrument Linearity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linearity describes how closely instrument output follows a linear relation to input over a defined range. An instrument can be precise but nonlinear, and a suitable nonlinear calibration may still make it useful.
required_concepts: Response agreement with a linear model over a stated range.
major_error_concepts: Calling every nonlinear instrument unusable without considering calibrated nonlinear models.

cards.prompt: What is Offset Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An offset error is an additive output or inferred-input shift in a simple calibration model. Subtracting a known offset can correct its estimate, while uncertainty in that correction remains part of the result.
required_concepts: Additive calibration shift with residual correction uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Assuming subtracting an estimated offset makes its uncertainty vanish.

cards.prompt: What is Gain Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A gain error changes the scale factor between input and output in a measurement model. It differs from an additive zero offset, so measurements over a range are needed to separate their effects.
required_concepts: Multiplicative calibration-scale error.
major_error_concepts: Correcting a scale error by subtracting one constant at every input without justification.

cards.prompt: What is Drift? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Drift is a change in instrument response or baseline over time under nominally similar input. Repeated references or time-aware models can reveal it, while short-run scatter alone may underestimate its effect.
required_concepts: Time-dependent response or baseline change.
major_error_concepts: Treating a slowly moving baseline as independent zero-mean noise that always averages away.

cards.prompt: What is Hysteresis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Hysteresis makes an instrument's output depend on its input history as well as its current input. Approaching the same input from above and below can therefore produce different readings under the same nominal value.
required_concepts: History-dependent measurement response.
major_error_concepts: Assuming current input alone determines output in a device with hysteresis.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Loading? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Loading occurs when a measuring device changes the system it measures, such as a finite-resistance voltmeter drawing current. The instrument must be included in the model if its influence is not negligible relative to the desired uncertainty.
required_concepts: Measurement apparatus perturbs the target system.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a measurement is noninvasive merely because the device is called a meter.

cards.prompt: What is Instrument Response Time? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Response time characterizes how quickly an instrument follows a changed input. A slow sensor can smooth or delay true changes, so its transient response matters when the measurand varies on a comparable timescale.
required_concepts: Instrument temporal response limits measurement of changes.
accepted_variants: Sensor time constant or settling behavior.
major_error_concepts: Treating a delayed sensor trace as the undistorted instantaneous input.

cards.prompt: What is Instrument Bandwidth? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Bandwidth specifies the frequency range over which an instrument meets a stated response criterion. Amplitude and phase both matter; one cutoff number alone does not describe every feature of its frequency response.
required_concepts: Frequency-dependent response with explicit criterion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sensor reproduces all phase and amplitude information perfectly below a vaguely stated maximum frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Noise? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Noise is unwanted variation relative to the specified signal model and measurement objective. Its spectrum, distribution, and correlations determine how filtering or averaging affects the measurement.
required_concepts: Unwanted modeled signal variation with statistical structure.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all noise is independent Gaussian white noise without evidence or a model.

cards.prompt: What is Signal-to-Noise Ratio? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Signal-to-noise ratio compares a defined signal measure with a corresponding noise measure. Power and amplitude ratios require different logarithmic conventions, and the bandwidth used to measure noise must be stated.
required_concepts: Defined signal and noise measures with bandwidth and ratio convention.
major_error_concepts: Comparing two SNR values obtained over different noise bandwidths as though they were automatically equivalent.

cards.prompt: What is Sample Mean? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The sample mean is the arithmetic average of measured values. It estimates a common expected value under appropriate assumptions, but changing conditions or unequal measurement targets can make a pooled mean misleading.
required_concepts: Average estimates a specified common mean only with suitable assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Averaging measurements of changing physical conditions and labeling the result one unchanged-state measurement without qualification.

cards.prompt: What is Sample Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sample variance describes dispersion around the sample mean, commonly using denominator n-1 for the usual unbiased IID variance estimate. The estimator's interpretation changes when dependence or nonidentical distributions matter.
required_concepts: Squared spread with stated denominator and sampling assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming n-1 makes a variance estimate universally unbiased for every dependent or drifting dataset.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Deviation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and describes observation spread in the original units. It is not the same as uncertainty of the mean, which can be smaller under independent repeated measurements.
required_concepts: Observation spread in original units.
major_error_concepts: Reporting individual-observation standard deviation as necessarily equal to standard error of an average.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For n independent identically distributed observations with finite variance, the mean's standard error is sigma/sqrt(n), estimated by s/sqrt(n). Dependence, common offsets, and drift are not removed by using this formula blindly.
required_concepts: Mean uncertainty shrinks as sqrt(n) under IID assumptions.
accepted_variants: Standard error of the sample mean.
major_error_concepts: Reducing common systematic uncertainty by sqrt(n) solely because many readings were taken.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Independence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Independence means the joint probability law factors into separate laws for the observations or variables. Zero correlation is weaker in general, and repeated readouts of the same slowly changing process may be dependent.
required_concepts: Joint factorization, not merely zero correlation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming measurements are independent because they were stored in separate data rows.

cards.prompt: What is Covariance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Covariance measures joint linear variation about means and has units equal to the product of the variables' units. Shared calibration or environmental effects can produce covariance between derived or separately recorded values.
required_concepts: Joint centered-product expectation with product units.
major_error_concepts: Assuming separate instruments imply zero covariance despite a shared reference or environment.

cards.prompt: What is Correlation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Correlation normalizes covariance by both standard deviations and is dimensionless when variances are positive. It describes linear association, not proof of a causal mechanism or general independence when zero.
required_concepts: Normalized covariance and linear association only.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting zero correlation as proof of independence for arbitrary distributions.

cards.prompt: What is Uncertainty Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For small input uncertainties, first-order propagation gives Var(f) approximately gradient f transpose Sigma gradient f, where Sigma is the input covariance matrix. Independent-input quadrature is the special case with zero off-diagonal covariances.
required_concepts: Derivative sensitivity plus full input covariance.
major_error_concepts: Dropping covariance terms despite known shared-input uncertainties.

cards.prompt: What is Quadrature Combination? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Independent uncertainty contributions to a linearized sum combine through the sum of variances, so standard uncertainties combine in quadrature. Fully correlated contributions require their covariance and cannot generally use that independence rule.
required_concepts: Sum variances for independent contributions.
major_error_concepts: Adding all standard deviations in quadrature regardless of correlation.

cards.prompt: What is relative uncertainty for a nonzero measurement result, and how does it differ from percent error against a reference value?
cards.definition: For a nonzero estimate y with standard uncertainty u(y), relative standard uncertainty is u_r(y)=u(y)/abs(y). It is dimensionless and is expressed as a percentage by multiplying by 100. The same ratio can be used for another explicitly identified uncertainty measure, but its coverage meaning must be retained. It is undefined at y=0 and may be uninformative near zero. It describes uncertainty relative to the estimate, not a measured discrepancy from a known reference value.
required_concepts: Divide the stated absolute uncertainty by the magnitude of the nonzero estimate; multiply by 100 for percent uncertainty.
Relative uncertainty is not percent error against a reference, and the zero or near-zero denominator needs care.
accepted_variants: Fractional standard uncertainty is u/|y| for y not equal to zero; unlike relative error, it does not require knowing a true or reference value.
major_error_concepts: Making relative standard uncertainty negative just because the estimate is negative.
Defining uncertainty solely as deviation from a known reference value.
Treating u/0 as a finite relative uncertainty.

cards.prompt: What is Nonlinear Uncertainty Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nonlinear propagation can produce asymmetric or shifted output distributions even from symmetric input uncertainties. First-order derivative propagation can fail near singularities, thresholds, or strong curvature and is not automatically rescued by more printed digits.
required_concepts: Nonlinear models can invalidate symmetric first-order propagation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a symmetric input error bar always yields a symmetric output uncertainty interval.

cards.prompt: What is Monte Carlo Uncertainty Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Monte Carlo propagation samples a specified joint input uncertainty model and evaluates the measurement model repeatedly. It propagates the assumed uncertainties but does not discover missing systematic effects or validate the model automatically.
required_concepts: Simulation of the joint input model through the measurement equation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming many simulations establish that every relevant uncertainty source was included.

cards.prompt: What is Uncertainty Budget? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An uncertainty budget lists relevant input quantities, uncertainty estimates, distributions or covariance assumptions, and sensitivity to the reported measurand. It separates contributions so dominant limitations are visible without pretending the list is complete merely because it is tabulated.
required_concepts: Explicit sources, magnitudes, dependencies, and sensitivities.
major_error_concepts: Adding overlapping contributions twice while treating them as independent sources.

cards.prompt: What is Combined Standard Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A combined standard uncertainty summarizes the output spread in standard-deviation-like units under the stated uncertainty model. It is not automatically a specified coverage interval without additional distribution and coverage assumptions.
required_concepts: Combined output standard-scale uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Calling one standard uncertainty a universal 95 percent interval.

cards.prompt: What is Expanded Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An expanded uncertainty multiplies a combined standard uncertainty by a stated coverage factor. The associated coverage interpretation depends on the output distribution and degrees of freedom, so the factor and assumptions should accompany the result.
required_concepts: Coverage-factor expansion with stated interpretation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the same multiplier gives exact coverage for all distributions and sample sizes.

cards.prompt: What is Significant Figures? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Significant figures communicate the precision justified by a quantity's representation and uncertainty. They are a reporting convention, not a replacement for explicit uncertainty propagation or a proof of accuracy.
required_concepts: Reported digits should reflect justified uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Using significant-figure counting as a complete uncertainty analysis.

cards.prompt: What is Rounding Measurement Results? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Rounding should be applied consistently to the final reported value and uncertainty, while intermediate calculations retain enough precision to avoid avoidable numerical error. Extra intermediate digits do not imply extra physical certainty.
required_concepts: Preserve calculation precision and round the reported result consistently.
major_error_concepts: Rounding every intermediate step aggressively and assuming final results are unaffected.

cards.prompt: What is Confidence Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A frequentist confidence interval is produced by a procedure with stated repeated-sampling coverage under assumptions. The confidence level is not, by itself, a posterior probability that a fixed parameter lies in this one already observed interval.
required_concepts: Procedure-level coverage interpretation.
Not automatically a posterior probability.
major_error_concepts: Assigning the confidence level directly as a probability for the fixed parameter in one realized interval without a Bayesian model.

cards.prompt: What is Coverage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coverage is the fraction of repeated intervals that contain the target under the assumed data-generating and interval procedure. Nominal coverage can fail when bias, dependence, or model misspecification is ignored.
required_concepts: Repeated-interval target inclusion rate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a nominal 95 percent label guarantees actual coverage under any unmodeled systematic error.

cards.prompt: What is Bootstrap? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A bootstrap estimates sampling behavior by resampling data using a scheme appropriate to the observation design. Ordinary IID resampling is not automatically suitable for correlated time series, clustered measurements, or unmodeled drift.
required_concepts: Resampling must match data dependence and design.
major_error_concepts: Shuffling dependent points independently while claiming their time dependence was preserved.

cards.prompt: What is Likelihood? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A likelihood evaluates how a specified statistical model assigns probability or density to the observed data as parameters vary. It is a function of parameters given the observations, not generally a normalized probability distribution over parameters.
required_concepts: Observed-data model evaluated as a parameter function.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting an unnormalized likelihood as a posterior parameter probability without a prior and normalization.

cards.prompt: What is Least Squares? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Least squares fits parameters by minimizing squared residuals between observations and model predictions. It corresponds to a likelihood method for certain noise assumptions, but fitting alone does not establish the physical model or independence assumptions.
required_concepts: Minimize squared observation-prediction discrepancies.
major_error_concepts: Treating a small least-squares objective as proof of the proposed mechanism.

cards.prompt: What is Weighted Least Squares? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Weighted least squares uses weights reflecting the error model, commonly inverse variances for independent unequal-variance observations. Generalized least squares includes a full covariance matrix when residual errors are correlated.
required_concepts: Variance or covariance-aware residual weighting.
major_error_concepts: Using standard deviation rather than variance for inverse-variance weights without changing the objective.

cards.prompt: What is Errors in Variables? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Errors-in-variables methods account for uncertainty in predictors as well as responses. Ordinary least squares that treats a noisy predictor as exact can bias fitted slopes, so the relevant input uncertainty model matters.
required_concepts: Predictor uncertainty affects regression estimates.
major_error_concepts: Assuming moving all predictor uncertainty into vertical error bars always reproduces the correct fit.

cards.prompt: What is Residual? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A residual is an observed value minus the fitted prediction under a stated sign convention. Residual patterns can reveal model or noise problems, but fitted residuals are not identical to the true unobserved errors because parameters were estimated.
required_concepts: Observed-minus-fitted discrepancy.
Fitting affects residual properties.
major_error_concepts: Treating residuals as independent untouched noise draws automatically after model fitting.

cards.prompt: What is Chi-Squared Statistic? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A chi-squared fit statistic sums squared residuals scaled by their variance, or uses the inverse covariance quadratic form. Its reference distribution requires an appropriate noise model, covariance information, and treatment of fitted parameters.
required_concepts: Variance-scaled residual sum or covariance quadratic form.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting any arbitrary squared residual sum as having a chi-squared reference distribution without assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Reduced Chi-Squared? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reduced chi-squared is chi-squared divided by the relevant residual degrees of freedom. A value near one can be consistent with an appropriate model and uncertainty scale, but is not universal proof of correctness or a target to force by arbitrary rescaling.
required_concepts: Chi-squared per appropriate residual degree of freedom.
major_error_concepts: Adjusting error bars solely to make reduced chi-squared one and calling that independent validation.

cards.prompt: What is Residual Degrees of Freedom? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Residual degrees of freedom often equal independent observations minus fitted parameters in a regular full-rank linear fit. Constraints, dependence, and nonlinear or regularized procedures can change this simple counting or its interpretation.
required_concepts: Independent information minus fitted freedom in the regular case.
major_error_concepts: Using raw row count minus parameter count as exact for every correlated or constrained fit.

cards.prompt: What is Parameter Covariance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A parameter covariance matrix describes uncertainty and correlation among fitted parameters under the fit model. Marginal standard errors are square roots of diagonal entries, while off-diagonal entries affect uncertainties of combined predictions.
required_concepts: Joint fit-parameter uncertainty including correlations.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring parameter covariance when propagating a prediction that depends on several fitted parameters.

cards.prompt: What is Fit Parameter Correlation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Parameter correlation means different fitted parameter combinations can compensate for one another in the model. Strong correlation can make individual parameters poorly determined even when predictions within the measured range are relatively precise.
required_concepts: Compensating parameter combinations limit separate identification.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an apparently accurate fitted curve guarantees every parameter is individually precise.

cards.prompt: What is Model Adequacy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Model adequacy asks whether a model captures the observations well enough for the stated measurement purpose and uncertainty scale. Residual structure, physical assumptions, and the sampled range matter beyond one numerical fit score.
required_concepts: Purpose-specific agreement including residuals and physical assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a model adequate solely because a fitted line appears smooth.

cards.prompt: What is Model Comparison? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Model comparison weighs fit, complexity, and predictive or physical purpose using a stated criterion. A more flexible model can fit the same data better without providing better-supported physics or reliable extrapolation.
required_concepts: Compare fit and flexibility under a stated purpose.
major_error_concepts: Selecting the model with most parameters solely because its training residual is smallest.

cards.prompt: What is Linearization for Fitting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linearizing a physical relation by transforming variables can simplify plotting or fitting but also transforms its uncertainty distribution. Ordinary unweighted fitting after transformation can imply a different error model from fitting the original measurements.
required_concepts: Transformation changes both relation and error model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a log transform leaves additive constant-variance measurement errors unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Logarithmic Plot? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A logarithmic axis displays multiplicative changes as equal spacing, while plotting log-transformed values changes the fitted variable. Positive-domain restrictions and transformed uncertainties must be handled explicitly.
required_concepts: Log scale or transformation requires positive quantities and clear interpretation.
major_error_concepts: Taking a real logarithm of zero or negative baseline-subtracted data without a defined alternative model.

cards.prompt: What is Power-Law Fit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A power-law model y=A x^b becomes log y=log A+b log x for positive x and y. The straight-line slope estimates b only under the model and compatible transformed error treatment, not for any vaguely linear-looking log plot.
required_concepts: Power-law log slope and domain assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Inferring an exact physical scaling law solely from a short straight segment on log axes.

cards.prompt: What is Exponential Fit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An exponential model y=A exp(-t/tau)+b includes amplitude, timescale, and possibly a baseline. Taking a logarithm requires handling b first, and an uncertain baseline can strongly affect the inferred decay time.
required_concepts: Exponential dynamics with explicit baseline and error treatment.
major_error_concepts: Logging y directly when an important nonzero baseline is present and assuming the slope remains exactly -1/tau.

cards.prompt: What is Outlier? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An outlier is an observation unusual relative to a stated model or expected distribution. It can reflect a recording problem, a different regime, or genuine variation, so exclusion requires a defensible rule rather than the desire for a better fit.
required_concepts: Model-relative unusual observation with documented disposition.
major_error_concepts: Deleting points solely because they weaken the desired conclusion.

cards.prompt: What is Robust Estimation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Robust estimation reduces sensitivity to certain departures such as unusually large residuals. It changes the estimation rule and assumptions, but does not automatically correct calibration bias or justify ignoring physical anomalies.
required_concepts: Reduced influence of specified deviations.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a robust estimator repairs every systematic measurement effect.

cards.prompt: What is Missing Data? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Missing data are unobserved measurements whose absence may depend on conditions or outcomes. Treating missing values as zero or discarding them can change the estimand and bias a result if missingness is selective.
required_concepts: Absence mechanism can affect inference.
major_error_concepts: Substituting zero for every missing sensor value while claiming unchanged physical meaning.

cards.prompt: What is Censoring and Detection Limits? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Censoring records only that a value lies above or below a limit rather than its exact value. A detection-limit statement is not the same as a measured zero, and the likelihood should reflect the available interval information when relevant.
required_concepts: Threshold-limited value information.
major_error_concepts: Replacing every below-threshold value with an exact zero without accounting for the limit.

cards.prompt: What is Saturation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Saturation occurs when an instrument can no longer follow input changes within its output range, often clipping the response. Saturated readings do not preserve ordinary linear calibration and may provide only a bound on the true input.
required_concepts: Range-limited clipped response.
major_error_concepts: Fitting clipped peaks as undistorted amplitudes using the same linear gain.

cards.prompt: What is Quantization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Quantization maps a continuous input range into discrete output levels. A uniform-bin uncertainty model can be useful under stated conditions, but quantization error is not always independent white noise, especially for slowly varying or synchronized signals.
required_concepts: Discrete encoding of a continuous range.
major_error_concepts: Assuming quantization automatically creates independent random error with the same distribution for every signal.

cards.prompt: What is Analog-to-Digital Conversion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An analog-to-digital converter samples and quantizes an analog input with specified range, timing, and resolution. Effective measurement quality also depends on noise, reference stability, linearity, and input conditioning, not bit count alone.
required_concepts: Sampling plus quantization with hardware response limits.
major_error_concepts: Equating nominal ADC bits directly with achieved measurement accuracy.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Rate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sampling rate is the number of recorded samples per unit time under the stated timing convention. Irregular sampling requires actual timestamps rather than treating every pair of adjacent records as an equal time interval.
required_concepts: Samples per time with timing assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assigning one exact interval to irregularly timed data merely because rows are consecutive.

cards.prompt: What is Nyquist Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a bandlimited signal under ideal regular sampling assumptions, a sampling rate greater than twice the highest retained frequency permits reconstruction in the standard theorem. The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, and real filtering and margin requirements still matter.
required_concepts: Bandlimit and regular sampling underpin the twice-frequency condition.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any arbitrary unfiltered signal is fully reconstructable simply because some visible peak lies below half the sample rate.

cards.prompt: What is Aliasing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Aliasing occurs when different underlying frequencies become indistinguishable in sampled data. Frequency content above the usable sampled band can appear as false lower-frequency structure unless prevented or modeled appropriately.
required_concepts: Sampling confounds distinct frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an observed low-frequency digital peak must have originated at that same analog frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Anti-Alias Filtering? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An anti-alias filter limits input frequency content before sampling so unwanted high-frequency signals are not folded into the recorded band. Filtering afterward cannot generally identify and undo an alias that is already indistinguishable in the data.
required_concepts: Bandlimit before digitization.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a digital low-pass filter always recovers the original signal after arbitrary analog aliasing.

cards.prompt: What is Discrete Fourier Transform? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A discrete Fourier transform decomposes a finite sampled record into frequency-bin amplitudes, while an FFT is an efficient algorithm for that transform. Interpretation depends on sampling rate, record length, normalization, and windowing.
required_concepts: Finite-record frequency decomposition; FFT is the algorithm.
major_error_concepts: Treating FFT as a separate physical spectrum independent of sampling and finite-window assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Frequency Resolution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an evenly sampled record of duration T, the basic Fourier-bin spacing is approximately 1/T. Zero padding interpolates the displayed transform but does not add the independent time information needed to resolve arbitrarily close components.
required_concepts: Record duration sets fundamental frequency spacing.
major_error_concepts: Claiming zero padding alone creates the same resolving information as acquiring a longer record.

cards.prompt: What is Spectral Leakage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Spectral leakage spreads finite-record signal energy into neighboring Fourier bins when the observed waveform does not align with the implicit periodic extension. It is a windowing effect rather than necessarily additional physical oscillations.
required_concepts: Finite observation window spreads spectral energy.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting every neighboring spectral sidelobe as an independently excited physical mode.

cards.prompt: What is Window Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A window function weights a record before spectral analysis to manage leakage and sidelobes. It changes amplitude normalization, effective bandwidth, and resolution, so the chosen window must be reflected in quantitative interpretation.
required_concepts: Tapering trades sidelobes against resolution and normalization.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a window reduces leakage without changing any other spectral property.

cards.prompt: What is Power Spectral Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Power spectral density describes variance or power per unit frequency under a stated normalization. Integrating it over a band gives the corresponding band contribution, and one-sided versus two-sided conventions affect numerical factors.
required_concepts: Power or variance per frequency with explicit normalization.
major_error_concepts: Reading a spectral density bin value as total power without accounting for bandwidth.

cards.prompt: What is Autocorrelation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Autocorrelation measures association between a signal and its delayed version. It can reveal periodicity and dependence that affect averaging, but a finite noisy sample autocorrelation is only an estimate of the underlying structure.
required_concepts: Lagged self-correlation and dependence evidence.
major_error_concepts: Treating every nonzero empirical lag correlation as an exact underlying feature.

cards.prompt: What is Effective Sample Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An effective sample size summarizes the information about a specified estimator under dependence or weighting relative to a reference independent-sample model. It need not equal the number of stored points or one universal value for every statistic.
required_concepts: Estimator-specific information equivalent under dependence.
major_error_concepts: Using raw sample count in a sqrt(n) error reduction despite strong positive autocorrelation.

cards.prompt: What is Signal Averaging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Averaging repeated aligned measurements can reduce independent zero-mean noise while preserving a repeatable signal. It does not necessarily reduce coherent interference, common calibration error, or drift, and misalignment can blur the signal itself.
required_concepts: Averaging helps only appropriate noise components and alignment.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any unwanted component vanishes under enough repetitions regardless of correlation.

cards.prompt: What is Lock-In Detection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Lock-in detection correlates a measured signal with a known reference oscillation and low-pass filters the result to estimate a component's amplitude and phase. It rejects much out-of-band noise but not all interference at the reference frequency or systematic calibration error.
required_concepts: Reference-correlated narrowband amplitude and phase extraction.
major_error_concepts: Claiming lock-in detection removes every unwanted signal merely because a reference is used.

cards.prompt: What is Triggering? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A trigger defines when acquisition starts or how records are aligned to an event. Trigger thresholds, timing jitter, and selection rules can affect observed distributions, particularly when acquisition depends on the same signal being analyzed.
required_concepts: Event-based acquisition timing with possible selection effects.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a threshold trigger cannot bias the recorded amplitude distribution.

cards.prompt: What is Time Synchronization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Time synchronization aligns clocks or channels to a common timing model. Clock offset and drift can create apparent delays or phase shifts, so timestamp resolution alone does not establish synchronization accuracy.
required_concepts: Clock alignment includes offset and drift.
major_error_concepts: Equating many timestamp digits with known interchannel timing agreement.

cards.prompt: What is Randomization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Randomization assigns experimental conditions or run order through a chance mechanism to reduce systematic association with nuisance factors. It supports a stated inference design, but does not guarantee exact balance or remove every measurement bias in one finite experiment.
required_concepts: Chance assignment reduces systematic nuisance association.
major_error_concepts: Assuming randomized order corrects an uncalibrated scale factor automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Control Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A control condition provides a defined comparison that isolates a relevant change or background contribution. The control must match the causal or measurement question; an arbitrary convenient comparison may leave important differences uncontrolled.
required_concepts: Purpose-matched comparison condition.
major_error_concepts: Calling any unrelated reference measurement a sufficient control for the intended effect.

cards.prompt: What is Blocking? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Blocking groups runs with similar nuisance conditions and compares treatments within those groups. It can reduce unwanted variation while preserving the intended contrasts, provided the analysis reflects the blocking structure.
required_concepts: Group similar nuisance conditions and compare within blocks.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring block identity in an analysis where it materially changes the comparison and uncertainty.

cards.prompt: What is Independent Replication? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Independent replication repeats the relevant experimental unit or complete preparation to assess variability beyond readout noise. Repeated measurements on one unchanged unit answer a narrower question and should be labeled separately.
required_concepts: Repeat independent experimental units or preparations.
major_error_concepts: Counting repeated sensor reads of one specimen as many independently prepared specimens.

cards.prompt: What is Pseudoreplication? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Pseudoreplication treats dependent subsamples or repeated readings as independent experimental replicates. It can underestimate uncertainty and overstate evidence because the number of independently assigned or prepared units is smaller than the row count.
required_concepts: False independence from subsampling or repeated reads.
major_error_concepts: Using every time point from one treatment unit as a separately randomized treatment replicate.

cards.prompt: What is Blinding? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Blinding withholds condition labels or expected answers from people making relevant measurements or analysis choices when feasible. It can reduce expectation-driven decisions but does not replace calibration, randomization, or a valid model.
required_concepts: Hide influential labels to limit expectation effects.
major_error_concepts: Assuming blinded labels alone establish freedom from all systematic errors.

cards.prompt: What is Confounding? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A confounder is a factor whose variation is entangled with the intended explanatory change, preventing the observed difference from being uniquely attributed to that change under the design. Recording a confounder does not automatically remove its effect.
required_concepts: Competing factor inseparable from intended contrast.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a causal effect from two conditions that also differ in an uncontrolled influential variable.

cards.prompt: What is Interaction Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the setting of another in the stated response model. It is not captured by adding two constant independent main effects when that model's interaction term matters.
required_concepts: Factor effect varies with another factor's level.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a joint response must equal the sum of separate effects without checking the interaction model.

cards.prompt: What is Factorial Design? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A factorial design varies combinations of multiple factors to estimate main effects and interactions. Its size and interpretation depend on the levels, replication, and any deliberate fractionation, not just changing one factor at a time.
required_concepts: Combined factor-level settings reveal interactions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming one-factor-at-a-time measurements necessarily identify every interaction.

cards.prompt: What is Pilot Experiment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A pilot experiment tests feasibility, signal scale, timing, or analysis assumptions on a limited basis before a larger run. It can inform planning but does not automatically provide independent confirmatory evidence for choices tuned to that pilot.
required_concepts: Small feasibility and planning study with exploratory role.
major_error_concepts: Using pilot-tuned results as untouched confirmation without acknowledging the tuning.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Protocol? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measurement protocol specifies preparation, settings, sequence, recording, and analysis rules sufficiently for the intended repetition. Changes during a run should be recorded rather than retroactively presenting the whole run as one unchanged procedure.
required_concepts: Explicit procedure and recorded deviations.
major_error_concepts: Silently changing settings after seeing outcomes while reporting a single fixed protocol.

cards.prompt: What is Laboratory Notebook? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A laboratory notebook records observations, settings, decisions, and unexpected events with their context and timing. It preserves what actually happened, including unsuccessful runs, rather than only a polished reconstruction of favorable results.
required_concepts: Contemporaneous context-rich record of actual work.
major_error_concepts: Removing failed runs from the record merely because they are inconvenient for the final narrative.

cards.prompt: What is Raw Data? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Raw data are the original recorded observations before later transformations or discretionary exclusions. Preserving them separately from processed outputs allows corrections and analysis changes to be reconstructed without silently overwriting the original evidence.
required_concepts: Preserve original observations distinct from transformed data.
major_error_concepts: Overwriting original readings with corrected values while keeping no record of the change.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Metadata? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement metadata describe the conditions needed to interpret observations, including units, timestamps, instrument settings, calibration identifiers, and sample identity. A numerical table without this context may be impossible to interpret reliably.
required_concepts: Context needed to interpret recorded values.
major_error_concepts: Assuming unitless values and unknown instrument settings are sufficient for later quantitative interpretation.

cards.prompt: What is Data Provenance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Data provenance tracks how an observation or derived result came from its source through processing steps. It includes the relevant transformations, versions, and selections, not just the final plot filename.
required_concepts: Trace derivation from original data through transformations.
major_error_concepts: Claiming provenance from a final output alone without knowing which inputs or corrections produced it.

cards.prompt: What is Recomputable Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Recomputable analysis specifies inputs, code or calculation rules, parameters, and relevant software context so the same analysis can be rerun. Recomputing the same data is distinct from independently replicating the physical experiment.
required_concepts: Recreate calculation from preserved inputs and rules.
Different from new experimental replication.
major_error_concepts: Calling a successful rerun on identical data independent evidence from a newly performed experiment.

cards.prompt: What is Out-of-Sample Prediction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An out-of-sample prediction uses a fitted model to predict observations not used to tune it. It tests a different aspect of performance from residual fit on the training observations and must preserve the stated information boundary.
required_concepts: Predictions on observations not used for fitting or tuning.
major_error_concepts: Tuning repeatedly on a test set while continuing to call it untouched out-of-sample evidence.

cards.prompt: What is Null Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A null measurement seeks a balance or zero difference rather than inferring the target only from a large absolute deflection. It can reduce sensitivity to selected calibration factors but still depends on reference quality, detector resolution, and remaining systematic effects.
required_concepts: Balance-based measurement with selective uncertainty advantages.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a zero indication proves an exact zero physical difference regardless of offset and resolution.

cards.prompt: What is Instrument Intercomparison? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Instrument intercomparison measures the same defined quantity with different instruments or methods under matched conditions. Agreement is useful but can hide shared calibration biases, while disagreement must be interpreted using combined uncertainty and measurand alignment.
required_concepts: Compare methods on the same defined target.
Shared errors can conceal disagreement with truth.
major_error_concepts: Claiming two instruments agreeing proves both are accurate despite sharing an incorrect reference.

cards.prompt: What is Units of Fitted Parameters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A fitted parameter's units follow from the measurement model and chosen axes. Rescaling an axis changes numerical slopes and intercepts, so fitted coefficients should retain units and conversion history.
required_concepts: Model and axis units determine parameter units.
major_error_concepts: Comparing slopes measured in different units as numerically equivalent without conversion.

cards.prompt: What is Pendulum Measurement Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A small-angle pendulum measurement infers gravitational acceleration from the relation T squared=4pi squared L/g under the ideal model. Length definition, amplitude, timing response, and departures from the point-mass pendulum model contribute uncertainty or bias.
required_concepts: Infer g from ideal small-angle period-length relation.
Model and length/timing definitions matter.
major_error_concepts: Treating large-amplitude or poorly defined-length motion as exact small-angle data without correction.

cards.prompt: What is Spring-Stiffness Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A spring measurement estimates stiffness from force versus displacement in the linear elastic regime. A zero offset, preload, loading direction, or nonlinear extension can affect the fitted relation, so an intercept should not be forced away without physical justification.
required_concepts: Stiffness from linear force-displacement slope.
major_error_concepts: Forcing a line through the origin despite a known offset or preload and calling the slope unbiased.

cards.prompt: What is Momentum-Balance Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A momentum-conservation experiment compares total system momentum before and after an interaction while considering external impulse. Sensor alignment, sign conventions, timing, and the chosen system boundary affect the inferred momentum balance.
required_concepts: Compare total vector momentum with external impulse considered.
major_error_concepts: Calling any component-level mismatch a conservation violation while ignoring external forces or coordinate signs.

cards.prompt: What is Energy-Balance Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An energy-balance experiment accounts for relevant stored energies and transfers across a declared system boundary. Missing heat, friction, deformation, or sensor work can explain an apparent mechanical-energy shortfall without violating total energy conservation.
required_concepts: Track storage and transfers across the chosen boundary.
major_error_concepts: Equating nonconservation of measured mechanical energy alone with failure of total energy conservation.

cards.prompt: What is Resistance Measurement Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A resistance measurement relates terminal voltage and current under a suitable ohmic model. Meter loading, lead resistance, contact effects, and self-heating can change the inferred resistance from the intended sample value.
required_concepts: Voltage-current inference with circuit and thermal loading considered.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all measured voltage drops belong to the intended resistor while ignoring leads and contacts.

cards.prompt: What is RC Time-Constant Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An RC transient measurement estimates a relaxation time from capacitor voltage or current under the stated circuit model. Input waveform, source resistance, detector impedance, and baseline can alter the apparent time constant.
required_concepts: Fit RC dynamics with source and detector effects.
major_error_concepts: Equating a fitted exponential timescale with one nominal component product while ignoring measurement loading.

cards.prompt: What is Resonance Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A resonance measurement records a specified response amplitude or power versus drive frequency to estimate characteristic frequency and damping. Frequency resolution, drive stability, sweep settling, and the response variable's definition affect the inferred peak and width.
required_concepts: Frequency-response estimate with observable and settling specified.
major_error_concepts: Treating a rapidly swept unsatisfied transient as an exact steady-state resonance curve.

cards.prompt: What is Diffraction Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A diffraction measurement infers wavelength or geometry from a pattern using the relevant aperture and propagation model. Slit dimensions, angular calibration, finite source size, and near-versus-far-field assumptions contribute to the result.
required_concepts: Pattern-based inference requires correct geometry and diffraction regime.
major_error_concepts: Using a far-field small-angle formula as exact for every nearby screen geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Spectrometer Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A spectrometer calibration maps detector position or another readout to wavelength or frequency using suitable references. Instrument broadening and overlapping features must be separated from intrinsic spectral widths when interpreting lines.
required_concepts: Reference mapping from readout to spectrum.
Instrument response affects line shapes.
major_error_concepts: Calling every measured linewidth entirely intrinsic without considering instrument resolution.

cards.prompt: What is Calorimetric Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A calorimetric measurement uses a thermal energy balance including the sample, apparatus, and relevant losses. Response delays and phase changes can invalidate a simple one-body heat-capacity model if they are ignored.
required_concepts: Thermal balance includes apparatus, losses, and possible phase change.
major_error_concepts: Assigning all supplied energy to the sample while ignoring the container or surrounding heat exchange.

cards.prompt: What is Counting Experiment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A counting measurement records discrete events within a defined acquisition interval and selection rule. Counts depend on event rate, efficiency, live time, and background, so recorded count is not automatically the total number of physical events that occurred.
required_concepts: Discrete detection count with time, efficiency, and selection context.
major_error_concepts: Equating detected events with all emitted events without an efficiency model.

cards.prompt: What is Background Subtraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Background subtraction estimates a signal by removing an appropriately scaled background measurement. Uncertainty from both measurements and their scaling contributes, and shared effects can create covariance rather than independent errors.
required_concepts: Subtract scaled background and propagate both uncertainties.
major_error_concepts: Treating a measured background as exact while propagating only the signal-run counting error.

cards.prompt: What is Detector Dead Time? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Detector dead time is an interval after an event during which the system cannot record another event normally. Lost-count corrections depend on the dead-time model and rate; they are not always one universal linear adjustment.
required_concepts: Temporary event insensitivity with model-dependent count loss.
major_error_concepts: Assuming observed rate equals true rate at arbitrarily high event density despite finite detector recovery time.

cards.prompt: What is Poisson Count Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For independent events at a constant rate in the Poisson model, count variance equals expected count and standard deviation is its square root. Low counts, backgrounds, dead time, or changing rates require care beyond a symmetric sqrt(N) shorthand.
required_concepts: Poisson variance equals mean under independent constant-rate assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Reporting zero uncertainty from sqrt(0) as a complete upper-limit statement after observing no events.

cards.prompt: What is Ratio Measurements? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A ratio of measured signals can cancel some shared scale factors but also introduces denominator uncertainty and covariance. Near-zero denominators can produce strongly asymmetric or unstable uncertainty that simple fractional-error propagation misses.
required_concepts: Ratios can cancel shared effects but require denominator and covariance treatment.
major_error_concepts: Assuming normalizing by another measured signal removes all uncertainty automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Experimental Risk Boundary? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An experimental risk assessment identifies relevant hazards, exposure paths, equipment limits, and required safeguards before operation. A theoretical model or a successful data fit is not evidence that a physical setup is safe to operate.
required_concepts: Safety assessment is separate from measurement-model validity.
major_error_concepts: Treating successful simulation or fitting as sufficient proof of physical equipment safety.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Reporting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measurement report states the measurand, result, units, uncertainty interpretation, method, conditions, and material limitations. A bare number with many digits omits the information needed to interpret or compare the result.
required_concepts: Result plus context, uncertainty, method, and limitations.
major_error_concepts: Presenting a high-precision-looking number alone as a fully specified measurement.

cards.prompt: What is Experimental Claim Scope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A claim's scope should match the conditions, measurement range, and independent evidence actually obtained. Agreement for one setup or regime supports that bounded result, not automatic correctness across every instrument, parameter range, or physical model.
required_concepts: Conclusions bounded by tested conditions and evidence.
major_error_concepts: Generalizing one successful bounded experiment to all regimes without additional support.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Experimental Physics and Measurement.
